Subject: Hosted API latency expectations for production cutover

Hi Karthik,

Thanks again for the demo last week — FinServe is excited about the throughput gains on your hosted endpoints. Before we move forward with the purchase order, our infra team asked for explicit latency SLOs we can use in our runbook and procurement paperwork. A couple of specific asks:

- Can you confirm p50 and p95 tail latency targets for the hosted API for typical text-generation requests (prompt length ~150 tokens, response length ~200 tokens)?
- How do you measure those (rolling window, aggregation method)? What is the measurement window (e.g., 1m/5m/1h) and the percentile computation semantics?
- During regional incidents or capacity shortage do you offer temporary exceptions or credits instead of failing requests? If so, what are the guardrails?

If you have a short matrix (p50/p95 numbers + measurement windows + remediation/credit policy) you can share, that would speed our procurement process.

Appreciate a concise reply we can share with the SREs.

Best,
Claire Nguyen
Head of Platform Engineering
FinServe

Hi Claire — thanks for the clear list. Short answer up front: yes, we can commit to concrete p50/p95 targets for your production traffic profile and provide measurement details that match what your SREs need. Below is a concise SLO proposal for hosted API (we can iterate).

Proposed default SLOs (hosted API, gen endpoint, typical prompt/response sizes you specified):
- p50: <= 60 ms
- p95: <= 220 ms
Measurement and aggregation:
- Percentiles computed on a 5-minute sliding window, reported every 1 minute.
- Percentiles are calculated on server-side end-to-end request latency (time from request ingress to final token emitted), excluding client-side network.
- For our SLA/credits calculations we use a 24-hour rolling window and 5-minute buckets. The daily SLO pass is evaluated over those 5-minute bucket percentiles (standard query: group by 5m, compute p95 per bucket, then compute the fraction of buckets meeting target).

Exception policy (short):
- Regional capacity incidents: we route to next-best region when possible; if forced-fallbacks increase latency beyond p95 target we will document incident, provide mitigation timeline, and if the event breaches monthly uptime/latency guarantees we issue credits per the contract.
- Soft exceptions allowed for scheduled maintenance with 72-hour notice; emergency maintenance handled case-by-case.

I'll attach a short SLO matrix and the service definition. Looping in Laura from product who handles SLO wording for contracts.

Thanks,
Karthik Iyer
Account Exec, Redwood Inference

Claire — thanks for raising the measurement semantics question. A couple of clarifications from product/ops perspective that often come up with customers: 

1) Measurement semantics
- We measure per-request end-to-end server latency. For streaming responses we report time-to-first-token and time-per-subsequent-token separately. The p50/p95 numbers I quoted above refer to time-to-first-token unless you prefer an aggregated token-costed latency.
- Percentiles use HDR histograms internally to avoid skew from outliers and are computed using 5m buckets to balance noise vs. responsiveness.

2) Windowing for contractual evaluation
- Operational monitoring: 5-minute sliding window, reported 1m.
- Contractual pass/fail: 24-hour rolling window composed of 5-minute buckets. A day fails only if more than 3% of the 5-minute buckets in that 24h window exceed the p95 target. This is intentionally tolerant of short spikes but still enforces sustained degradation.

3) Exceptions and credits
- If we trigger our capacity fallback (auto-region reroute) and you see elevated latency, we commit to: incident report within 4 hours, mitigation ETA within 12 hours for non-catastrophic events, and SLA credit calculation per contract (example: > 8 hours of degraded daily availability = X% credit). We can surface a clause with exact numbers in the SOW.

If you want, Aditya from infra can provide empirical numbers from our hosted fleet for requests matching your token profile to validate these targets.

—Laura

Redwood Inference

Tom/Claire — quick empirical data from our hosted fleet for generative requests approximating your profile (prompt 150 tokens / response 200 tokens):

- Historical summary (30-day rolling):
  - p50: 54 ms (median)
  - p95: 185 ms
  - p99: 430 ms
- 90-day aggregate: p95 ~ 210 ms (variance driven by bursts on peak US-EAST morning traffic)

Streaming specifics (time-to-first-token / token emission rate):
- time-to-first-token p95: 160 ms
- token emission p95 (per-token median time): 8 ms/token at steady state; p95 token emission spikes to ~18 ms/token during CPU-constrained bursts.

Credit illustration (example, not final legal):
- If daily evaluation shows > 6% of 5-minute buckets exceed p95 target -> 10% monthly usage credit for impacted month.
- If > 20% of buckets exceed p95 target -> 30% monthly usage credit.

We can provide anonymized HDR histograms for the 30/90 day windows if that helps procurement. Also happy to include a clause that allows FinServe to specify a custom traffic profile for contractual verification during the onboarding period.

Next steps suggested:
- Karthik: confirm whether these numbers satisfy procurement or if they want stricter guarantees tied to reserved capacity (Dedicated).
- Laura: confirm final SLO wording for SOW; I can attach histograms when you sign off.

Thanks,
Aditya Rao
